questions.q: Ethylamine is a stronger base than ammonia because:
questions.solution:
The alkyl group's **positive inductive effect** pushes electron density onto the nitrogen, making its lone pair more available to accept a proton.

It also stabilises the resulting ammonium ion.
options: the ethyl group releases electrons to the nitrogen

questions.q: Phenylamine is a much weaker base than ethylamine because:
questions.solution:
The lone pair overlaps with the ring's $\pi$ system and is **delocalised**, so it is far less available to bond to a proton.

Protonating it would also destroy that delocalisation, which costs energy. $\text{p}K_{b}$: phenylamine $9.4$, ethylamine $3.3$.
options: the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the ring
it has a higher molar mass

questions.q: At its isoelectric point, an amino acid exists mainly as:
questions.solution:
A **zwitterion** — internally ionised as $\text{H}_{3}\text{N}^{+}\text{-CHR-COO}^{-}$, with no **net** charge.

That is why amino acids are high-melting crystalline solids, soluble in water and insoluble in organic solvents, quite unlike comparable amines or acids.

**Condensation** polymerisation — a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid join with the loss of a small molecule (water or HCl) at each link.

The resulting **amide** links are what make nylon a polyamide, like protein.

questions.q: The bond joining amino acids in a protein is:
questions.solution:
A **peptide bond**, $-\text{CO}-\text{NH}-$, formed by condensation between one amino acid's carboxyl group and the next one's amino group.

It has partial double-bond character, so it is planar and rigid — which is precisely what makes the $\alpha$-helix and $\beta$-sheet possible.

questions.q: How many isomeric amines has the formula $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{9}\text{N}$?
questions.solution: Propan-1-amine, propan-2-amine, N-methylethanamine and trimethylamine — $\mathbf{4}$: two primary, one secondary, one tertiary.

questions.q: How many peptide links are in a linear tetrapeptide?
questions.solution: $n - 1 = \mathbf{3}$ — like fence posts and the panels between them.

questions.q: How many different dipeptides can be made from two different amino acids, using each once per dipeptide and allowing either order?
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{2}$ — A-B and B-A. The order matters, because the two ends of an amino acid are different.

With 20 amino acids there are $400$ dipeptides, and the number of possible proteins is astronomically large.

questions.q: Find the molar mass of glycine, $\text{H}_{2}\text{NCH}_{2}\text{COOH}$, in g/mol. (C $= 12$, H $= 1$, N $= 14$, O $= 16$.)
How many water molecules are lost when five amino acids condense into a linear pentapeptide?
questions.solution: $\mathbf{4}$ — one for each of the four peptide links formed.

questions.q: Compare the basicity of ammonia, ethylamine and phenylamine, and explain how the basicity of a substituted phenylamine depends on the substituent.
questions.solution:
**The order: ethylamine $>$ ammonia $\gg$ phenylamine.**

$\text{p}K_{b}$: ethylamine $3.3$, ammonia $4.8$, phenylamine $9.4$ — phenylamine is about **forty thousand times** weaker than ethylamine.

**Ethylamine against ammonia.** The ethyl group **releases** electron density inductively, increasing the electron density on nitrogen and making the lone pair more available. It also stabilises the ethylammonium ion.

**Phenylamine against both.** The lone pair occupies a $p$ orbital that overlaps with the ring's $\pi$ system, so it is **delocalised over the ring** and is no longer fully available.

Protonation would also **destroy that delocalisation**, costing the stabilisation energy — so the reaction is doubly unfavourable.

**Substituent effects on phenylamine.**

• **Electron-withdrawing groups** ($-\text{NO}_{2}$, $-\text{CN}$, halogens) pull still more density away from the nitrogen, making it a **weaker** base. 4-nitrophenylamine is a very weak base indeed.

• **Electron-releasing groups** ($-\text{CH}_{3}$, $-\text{OCH}_{3}$) push density towards it, making it a **stronger** base.

• The effect is **largest from the ortho and para positions**, where resonance can reach the nitrogen. A meta substituent acts only inductively and matters much less.

**A general principle worth extracting.** Base strength depends on the **availability of the lone pair**; acid strength depends on the **stability of the conjugate base**. Both are questions about where electron density ends up.

questions.q: Describe the structure of an amino acid, explain zwitterions and the isoelectric point, and describe how a protein's primary structure is determined.
questions.solution:
**Structure.** $\text{H}_{2}\text{N-CHR-COOH}$ — an amino group and a carboxyl group on the **same** carbon, with a side chain R that differs between the twenty naturally occurring amino acids.

**All except glycine are chiral**, and biology uses only the L form.

**Zwitterions.** The carboxyl group is acidic and the amino group basic, so the proton transfers internally:

$\text{H}_{3}\overset{+}{\text{N}}\text{-CHR-COO}^{-}$

The molecule is internally ionised while remaining overall neutral, which is why amino acids are ionic solids melting above $200$°C rather than the low-boiling liquids their molar mass suggests.

**The isoelectric point** is the pH at which the zwitterion form predominates and there is **no net charge**.

• Below it, the $-\text{COO}^{-}$ takes a proton and the molecule becomes a **cation**.

• Above it, the $-\text{NH}_{3}^{+}$ loses one and it becomes an **anion**.

At the isoelectric point the amino acid does not migrate in an electric field, and its solubility is at a minimum.

**That is what makes electrophoresis work:** at a chosen pH different amino acids carry different charges and move at different rates, so a mixture separates into bands.

**Determining the primary structure.**

1. **Hydrolyse** the protein completely with $6$ M HCl at $110$°C, breaking every peptide link.

2. **Separate and identify** the amino acids by chromatography or electrophoresis, comparing $R_{f}$ values with standards.

3. To get the **sequence** rather than merely the composition, hydrolyse only partially into short fragments, sequence each, and reassemble from the overlaps.

questions.q: Compare addition and condensation polymerisation, describe the formation of nylon and Terylene, and explain why condensation polymers are biodegradable while addition polymers are not.
questions.solution:
**Addition polymerisation.** Many **unsaturated** monomers join with **no other product**. The backbone is C–C throughout, and the atom economy is $100\%$.

**Condensation polymerisation.** Monomers with **two functional groups each** join with the loss of a small molecule — usually water or HCl — at every link.

**Nylon-6,6 — a polyamide.** A diamine and a dicarboxylic acid:

$\text{H}_{2}\text{N}(\text{CH}_{2})_{6}\text{NH}_{2} + \text{HOOC}(\text{CH}_{2})_{4}\text{COOH} \to$ amide links $+ \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

Used for fibres, ropes, gears and parachutes.

**Terylene (PET) — a polyester.** A diol and a dicarboxylic acid:

$\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH} + \text{HOOC-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-COOH} \to$ ester links $+ \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

Used for clothing and drinks bottles.

**Why condensation polymers are biodegradable.** The amide and ester links are **polar** and can be **hydrolysed** — by acid, alkali, or enzymes in the environment. The chain is broken back into its monomers, which are then metabolised.

**Why addition polymers are not.** Their backbone is entirely **non-polar C–C and C–H bonds**, with nothing for a nucleophile or an enzyme to attack. Poly(ethene) survives for centuries.

**The same difference makes condensation polymers recyclable by depolymerisation** — PET bottles can be hydrolysed back to their monomers and repolymerised, which addition polymers cannot.

It is worth noticing that **proteins and DNA are condensation polymers**, and for exactly this reason: life needs polymers that can be taken apart again.

questions.q: Describe two methods of preparing a primary amine, and give three reactions of amines.
questions.solution:
**Preparation 1 — reduction of a nitrile.**

$\text{RCN} + 4[\text{H}] \xrightarrow{\text{LiAlH}_{4}\text{ or H}_{2}/\text{Ni}} \text{RCH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$

**This lengthens the carbon chain by one**, since the nitrile itself came from a halogenoalkane and cyanide. It gives a clean primary amine with no mixture.

**Preparation 2 — reduction of a nitro compound.** The standard route to aromatic amines:

$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NO}_{2} + 6[\text{H}] \xrightarrow{\text{Sn/conc. HCl}} \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NH}_{2} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

The product is formed as its salt and must be liberated with NaOH.

**Preparation 3 — ammonolysis of a halogenoalkane**, with excess ammonia. Cheap but poor: the product is itself nucleophilic, so a mixture of primary, secondary, tertiary amines and the quaternary salt results.

**Reactions of amines.**

1. **As a base:** with acids, forming salts.

$\text{CH}_{3}\text{NH}_{2} + \text{HCl} \to \text{CH}_{3}\text{NH}_{3}^{+}\text{Cl}^{-}$

2. **As a nucleophile:** with acyl chlorides, giving **amides**.

$\text{CH}_{3}\text{NH}_{2} + \text{CH}_{3}\text{COCl} \to \text{CH}_{3}\text{CONHCH}_{3} + \text{HCl}$

3. **With nitrous acid at $5$°C:** an aromatic amine gives a **diazonium salt**, the gateway to azo dyes; an aliphatic one gives nitrogen gas and an alcohol.

4. **Carbylamine test:** with chloroform and alcoholic KOH, a **primary** amine gives an isocyanide of appalling smell — a clean test for primary amines only.

questions.q: Describe the preparation of an azo dye from phenylamine, and explain why azo compounds are coloured.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — diazotisation.** Phenylamine in cold dilute hydrochloric acid, treated with sodium nitrite at $0$–$5$°C:

$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{NH}_{2} + \text{HNO}_{2} + \text{HCl} \to \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{N}_{2}^{+}\text{Cl}^{-} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

**The temperature is critical.** Above about $10$°C the diazonium salt decomposes to phenol and nitrogen gas, and the preparation is lost.

**Step 2 — coupling.** The diazonium salt is added to an electron-rich aromatic compound — phenol in alkaline solution, or another amine:

$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{N}_{2}^{+} + \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{O}^{-} \to \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{-N}{=}\text{N-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{OH}$

An intensely coloured **azo compound** forms immediately — yellow, orange or red, depending on the coupling partner.

**Why azo compounds are coloured.** The $-\text{N}{=}\text{N}-$ group joins the two aromatic rings into one **extended delocalised system** spanning the whole molecule.

The more extended the delocalisation, the **smaller** the energy gap between the highest occupied and lowest unoccupied orbitals — small enough for **visible** light to bridge it.

The molecule absorbs part of the visible spectrum, and we see the **complementary** colour.

**The same principle everywhere:** chlorophyll, beta-carotene and indigo are all extensively conjugated. Benzene itself, with only one ring, absorbs in the ultraviolet and is colourless.

**Why azo dyes matter commercially.** They are cheap, cover the whole spectrum, and bind well to fabric — over half of all commercial dyes are azo compounds. Adding $-\text{SO}_{3}\text{H}$ groups makes them water-soluble for dyeing cotton.
